title: 2027 UF Guide to AI in Science
text:
NoteThis was written by humans.



✨ But we provide links to helpful AI-generated content along the way.


AI is radically redefining the nature of scientific inquiry — for better and for worse.
In Fall 2026, faculty, graduate students, and postdocs across multiple departments at the University of Florida came together to understand this urgent development. In a seminar titled Collective [Artificial] Intelligence in Science, we documented and discussed how AI is changing each component of our research workflow. This includes project management, idea development, data analysis, writing, and dissemination. To push our understanding, we alternated between the perspectives of an AI zealot and an AI critic — identifying key resources, consensus statements, and areas of disagreement along the way. The result is the 2027 UF Guide to AI in Science.
The seminar began with an introduction to big-team science — its rise1, competitive advantages2, and relevance to the current moment. For instance, the paper describing OpenAI’s GPT-1 had 4 authors3; the paper describing GPT-3 had 31 authors4; and the paper describing GPT-5 had 483 authors5 (Figure 1). Similarly, a prominent AI-led cybersecurity attack on the online community, Hugging Face, involved coordinated action among not one but thousands of AI agents6.








Figure 1: Credited co-authors on flagship AI model reports from OpenAI, Google, and Meta, 2018–2025. One square is one credited person; each block’s area is its author list.





After reviewing these developments, the course itself became a large-scale collaboration, dedicated to understanding how AI is changing the nature of science. Each week followed a consistent structure (Figure 2). First, we would select a component of the research pipeline to examine (e.g., data analysis). Second, we would spend one week compiling resources for understanding the emerging role of AI in that part of the research pipeline. Third, we would engage in peer-to-peer teaching. Last, we would use a live online voting platform to solicit, debate, and vote upon key resources and takeaways for the week7,8. Through these exercises, seminar participants received hands on experience with large-scale collaboration9,10. Along the way, not only developed and debated their personal philosophy statements – but also the general direction of AI at UF. Their results culminate into this 2027 UF Guide to AI in Science: a summary of our top resources, takeaways, and disagreements.






Figure 2: Structure of the UF Fall 2026 seminar, titled Collective [Artificial] Intelligence in Science.

title: Ideation and Project Management: Using AI
text:
Areas of consensus — and dissensus
Many researchers’ first contact with AI tools is in the realm of ideation or project management (Figure 1). For example, an in-class demo focused on an AI-assisted workflow for managing research trainee projects. More specifically, one seminar participant has their trainees submit weekly updates to a folder shared with the LLM, Claude (Figure 2, Panel A). This allows them to later prompt the model with questions about past conversations, challenges, decisions, and solutions (Figure 2, Panel B). Specifically, the seminar participant demonstrated how Claude can be used to efficiently take stock of a trainee’s progress, have a conversation with the LLM about potential future directions, and generate a simulated figure to send back to the trainee to convey next steps (Figure 2, Panel C).
The resources compiled by seminar participants illustrate that AI is a tool that is increasingly being used to expand ideation and project management capabilities (Figure 1). For example, as early as 2025, researchers documented that LLMs were capable of generating research ideas that were judged more novel than those of human experts1. These capabilities can be further improved by integrating causal discovery algorithms. More specifically, LLMs can efficiently extract which causal relationships have been reported in past research. When mapped across studies, causal discovery algorithms can be used to identify gaps in causal network maps — i.e., potential future research directions2. Such results highlight the increasing sophistication with which researchers are deploying AI to organize information, extract ideas, and even develop theory3.
Disagreement is common when researchers collaborate4,5 — and our seminar discussion was marked by both consensus and dissensus.
In terms of consensus, there was broad agreement that LLMs can assist with ideation, project management, and the organization of information. There was also broad agreement that this is changing the nature of competition in science — placing more emphasis on who can better leverage these tools for ideation and execution.
Yet, there was clear disagreement about how far things should go. Seminar participants strongly disagreed about whether AI is reliably superior at ideation, whether the institution of science should shift to more AI-led work, and whether humanity should strive for fully autonomous AI scientists. These disagreements echo throughout the scientific landscape, with recent back-to-back Nature pieces on both the capabilities6 and limitations7 of science with fewer humans and more AI. These limitations became the focus of the following week of the Fall 2026 Collective [Artificial] Intelligence Seminar (see Ideation and Project Management: Critiquing AI).
Figure 2: A seminar participant shared an LLM-assisted workflow to compile past meeting notes from their trainee (Panel A), review progress (Panel B), and mock a figure illustrating future directions (Panel C).

title: Ideation and Project Management: Critiquing AI
text:
Areas of consensus — and dissensus
In February 2026, an engineer running an online educational program used Claude Code to help launch a new side project. Instead of launching something new, they ultimately deleted everything they had already built: servers, networks, and years’ worth of datasets. The failure point, the engineer would later suggest, was over-automation1. The engineer never checked whether backups could be restored; they never pushed back on questionable recommendations from the coding agent; and they allowed it to run irreversible commands completely unsupervised. Issues like these are bound to become more common as scientists increasingly rely on AI — the focus of Week 3 of the Fall 2026 Collective [Artificial] Intelligence Seminar (Figure 1).
This week’s most popular resources focused on the pitfalls of using AI for ideation and project management (Figure 1). For example, one study used electroencephalography to measure brain connectivity patterns while writing alone, with a search engine, or with an LLM. Results suggested that LLM users exhibited the lowest levels of distributed brain activity — an index of lower cognitive engagement2. Similarly, when researchers rely more on AI for routine tasks like reproducibility checks, they catch fewer errors, propose weaker robustness checks, and ultimately move slower3. As scientists continue this shift towards AI, collective implications emerge. For instance, an analysis of 41 million research papers suggests that the adoption of AI tools and methods increases productivity, impact, and career outcomes for individuals — but at the expense of an overall narrowing of the scope of science4 (Figure 2).
Particularly after focusing a prior week on the benefits of AI, seminar discussion was marked by areas of consensus and dissensus5,6.
In general, there was strong agreement that concerns about AI have evolved beyond hallucination proneness7. Decreased vigilance and a collective narrowing of science received more attention among seminar participants — with near-unanimous agreement that maximizing value from AI requires training, practice, and refinement8. Yet, there was clear disagreement about the magnitude of the issue. Does AI hinder more than help with critical thinking? In the midst of widespread concerns about the robustness of existing research practices9, to what extent should we aim for increases in productivity? Last, is a narrowing of the scope of science necessarily a bad tradeoff10? After all, depression, addiction, cancer, dementia, climate change, and polarization are arguably enduring problems in need of sustained focus. Whether those problems are solved more quickly through increases in individual productivity, decreases in collective scope, and a faster overall science remains an open question.
